lesson.title: que as the Master Connector
lesson.subtitle: Why Spanish uses que for BOTH people and things (el hombre que habla, el café que quiero), never dropping 'that'

hook.title: One Word for 'Who', 'Whom', 'Which', and 'That'
hook.content: English makes you choose between 'the friend WHO lives in Madrid' and 'the house THAT is in Madrid'. In Spanish, unaccented **que** does BOTH jobs: el amigo que vive en Madrid, la casa que está en Madrid!

pattern.title: Never Drop 'Que'!
pattern.content: Whenever English drops 'that' ('the reservation I confirmed', 'the coffee you want'), your Spanish sentence MUST include que: la reservación que confirmé, el café que quieres.

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:
exercises.target_answer: el amigo que habla español, el café que quiero, la ciudad que visito, la casa que está aquí
exercises.meaning: the friend who speaks Spanish, the coffee (that) I want, the city that I visit, the house that is here
exercises.explanation: que connects both human and non-human nouns to a following clause.

exercises.prompt: Translate 'The friend who lives in Madrid':
options: El amigo que vive en Madrid
exercises.target_answer: El amigo que vive en Madrid
exercises.meaning: The friend who lives in Madrid
exercises.explanation: Use que (not quien) directly after the noun for 'who'.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The house that I want is big'
exercises.target_answer: La casa que quiero es grande
exercises.meaning: The house that I want is big
exercises.explanation: La casa + que quiero + es grande.

exercises.idea: say: 'It is the city that I want to visit'
cues: It is the city → Es la ciudad
that I want to visit → que quiero visitar
idea_parts: It is the city → Es la ciudad
that I want to visit → que quiero visitar
exercises.target_answer: Es la ciudad que quiero visitar
exercises.meaning: It is the city that I want to visit
exercises.explanation: Es la ciudad que quiero visitar.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: El amigo que vive aquí es muy bueno
exercises.target_answer: El amigo que vive aquí es muy bueno
exercises.meaning: The friend who lives here is very good
cues: The friend who: El amigo que
is very good: es muy bueno
exercises.explanation: El amigo que vive aquí es muy bueno.

summary.outcome: Connect relative clauses to both people and things using unaccented que.

use_example.german: El amigo que vive aquí tiene el libro que quiero.
use_example.english: The friend who lives here has the book that I want.

summary.takeaway: Whether the noun is a person ('who') or a thing ('that/which'), reach for que.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([2802] lo que: The Thing That / What): master neuter lo que at the start and middle of sentences.

qué.etymology_derivation: Latin quid → qué. Stressed in questions (accented qué), unstressed as conjunction (que).

hermano.context_phrase: Tengo un hermano y una hermana.
hermano.context_translation: I have a brother and a sister.
hermano.etymology_derivation: Latin germānus ('of the same seed/parents', English 'germane') lost its initial g- in Spanish: hermano!

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

casa.etymology_derivation: Latin casa originally meant a cottage, replacing domus in everyday Romance speech.

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

vivir.etymology_derivation: Latin vīvere — English vivid, revive, survive.

hablar.english_meaning: to speak, to talk (hablo: I speak)
hablar.etymology_derivation: Latin fabulārī (to converse, tell stories — English fable and fabulous) shifted initial f- to silent h-: hablar!

querer.etymology_derivation: Latin quaerere ('to seek, ask for') evolved in Spanish to 'to want' and 'to love'. When you make an inquiry in English, you are asking what you want.
